summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base used by network management protocols, with objects for managing a client of the iSCSI protocol (SCSI over TCP). It was a standards-track document and has been replaced by RFC 7147.

eli5.summary: A MIB is a standard list of dials and gauges a management tool can read. This one lists the dials and gauges for a computer that uses a network to talk to storage disks.

subtitle: SNMP objects for managing SCSI storage over TCP networks

tldr.problem: Organizations use iSCSI to access storage disks and tapes over regular IP networks instead of specialized storage networks, but need standardized management tools to monitor and configure iSCSI devices.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an SNMP MIB module for iSCSI that supplies objects for configuring instances, portals, nodes, targets, initiators, sessions, and connections, plus tables for statistics on login attempts, errors, and connection performance.
tldr.outcome: Network and storage administrators can now monitor and manage iSCSI initiators and targets using SNMP, tracking session performance and troubleshooting connection problems. RFC 7147 later updated this specification.

facts.value: Instance, Portal, Node, Target, Initiator, Session, Connection

today: RFC 4544 is a Proposed Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 7147, which updates the iSCSI MIB specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4544 defines an SNMP MIB module for managing iSCSI (Internet Small Computer System Interface) devices. iSCSI is a protocol that carries SCSI storage commands and data over TCP/IP networks, letting computers access disks and tape libraries over regular Ethernet instead of specialized storage area networks (SANs).

An iSCSI device can act as an initiator (like a computer requesting storage), a target (like a storage server providing disks), or both. The MIB module allows management stations to configure and monitor iSCSI instances, portals, nodes, sessions, and connections on these devices.

The MIB is designed to work alongside other MIB modules: the SCSI MIB for SCSI-layer information, the TCP MIB for connection-level details, and the IPS Identity Authentication MIB for credential management.
sections.eli5: iSCSI is a way to use the regular internet to send storage commands. This MIB lets you watch those connections working and adjust settings.

sections.title: iSCSI Concepts
sections.content:
The iSCSI MIB organizes information hierarchically. An iSCSI Instance is a distinct iSCSI entity on the managed device; most devices have one, but the module allows multiple instances for virtual or partitioned systems.

An iSCSI Portal is an IP address and TCP port that an iSCSI device listens on (if it acts as a target) or uses to initiate connections (if it acts as an initiator). Each portal can be marked for target role, initiator role, or both.

An iSCSI Node is an initiator, target, or both, identified by an iSCSI name. A Target node exports storage; an Initiator node requests access. Initiators and targets can have authorization lists that control who can connect to them.

An iSCSI Session is an active conversation between an initiator and a target. A session may consist of one or more Connections, each running over a separate TCP connection. Sessions can be inbound (an external initiator connecting to our target) or outbound (our initiator connecting to an external target).
sections.eli5: An instance is the whole iSCSI system. Portals are numbered doors. Nodes are computers or storage devices. Sessions are conversations. Connections are the phone lines carrying those conversations.

sections.title: Configuration and Tables
sections.content:
The iSCSI MIB module exports tables for each major object type. The iscsiInstanceAttributesTable holds vendor, version, and instance configuration. The iscsiPortalAttributesTable lists IP addresses and TCP transport settings, while iscsiTgtPortalAttributesTable and iscsiIntrPortalAttributesTable hold target and initiator-specific portal parameters.

The iscsiNodeAttributesTable describes iSCSI nodes, and iscsiTargetAttributesTable and iscsiInitiatorAttributesTable hold role-specific information. Authorization lists are stored in iscsiTgtAuthAttributesTable and iscsiIntrAuthAttributesTable.

The iscsiSessionAttributesTable describes active sessions, and iscsiConnectionAttributesTable describes TCP connections within those sessions. Management stations can create, modify, and delete rows in these tables to configure iSCSI devices.
sections.eli5: Different tables hold information about instances, doors, computers, storage, who's allowed to connect, active conversations, and the phone lines between them.

sections.title: Statistics and Monitoring
sections.content:
Beyond configuration tables, the iSCSI MIB provides statistics tables that augment the main tables. Each major object type has one or more statistics tables that track performance and errors.

Login statistics count successful and unsuccessful login attempts for targets and initiators. Logout statistics count normal and abnormal logouts. Session error statistics track digest errors, connection errors, and iSCSI format errors. Session performance statistics count requests, responses, and bytes transferred.

Connection error statistics track issues specific to individual TCP connections. The module includes both standard 32-bit counters and 64-bit high-capacity counters for high-volume environments. These statistics help operators identify performance bottlenecks, diagnose connectivity problems, and optimize iSCSI deployments.
sections.eli5: Statistics tables count successful connections, failed logins, messages sent, bytes transferred, and problems seen.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The iSCSI MIB exposes sensitive network information. Write-accessible objects in the portal, authorization, and target tables could allow unauthorized users to add or remove IP addresses, change access controls, or disable targets. Readable objects reveal the names and configurations of storage targets and initiators, helping attackers identify how to compromise the storage network.

However, the RFC notes that authentication of initiators and targets is the responsibility of the iSCSI protocol itself, defined in RFC 3720, not this MIB module.

The RFC strongly recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security for all access. Older SNMP versions lack proper authentication and encryption. Operators must ensure SNMP access controls restrict management objects to authorized users only.
sections.eli5: These settings control your storage network, so only trusted people should read or change them. Use the newest, most secure version of SNMP.
